nodes.label: Gregory S. Kealey
nodes.date_label: ‘The Honest Workingman’ 1976 · ‘The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing’ 1978 · Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism 1980 · ‘Prospects in the 1980s’ 1981 · Dreaming of What Might Be (with Palmer) 1982 · ‘1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt’ 1984 · Class, Gender, and Region 1988 · RCMP Security Bulletins (with Whitaker) 1989–97 · Spying on Canadians 2017
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of the working class, and later of political policing, who argued for putting class at the centre of Canadian history. Of Toronto's craftsmen he wrote that 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized', amounting to 'a high degree of workers' control of production' (1976); in 1981 he held that 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history', and he criticised the regional turn, under which 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere', as he had criticised the 'so-called "limited identities"' in 1978. David Brody, reviewing Toronto Workers Respond to Industrial Capitalism (1980), found it marked by 'what might be termed the Gutman school' and a useful foundation, but judged that Kealey had 'overreached himself' in its interpretation; Bettina Bradbury (1987) faulted him and Bryan Palmer for partially dismissing a Knights of Labor editor's picture of the ideal working-class wife as 'crude moralizing', and Joan Sangster (2000) found in both men's early books 'a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere'. From the late 1980s he edited the RCMP's security bulletins with Reg Whitaker and studied state surveillance of labour and the left, concluding that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (1992).

nodes.label: Sylvia Van Kirk
nodes.date_label: “Many Tender Ties” 1980 · “The Reputation of a Lady” 1986 · “Tracing the Fortunes of Five Founding Families of Victoria” 1997–98 · “From ‘Marrying-In’ to ‘Marrying-Out’” 2002
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of women in fur-trade society and of families of mixed descent in colonial Red River and Victoria. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) treated traders' marriages with Indigenous and later mixed-descent women, à la façon du pays, as the core of a fur-trade society; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the book set out to show that the trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity' and claimed support for 'the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation'. Her later articles turn on race and gender: the missionaries' 'racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women' and the rivalry among women 'compounded by the issue of race' in Red River (1986), and an acculturation in early Victoria that was 'gendered' (1997–98). Reviewers paired the book with Jennifer Brown's Strangers in Blood from 1981. One found its picture of fur-trade unions 'may be too complimentary', and Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Brown, Trigger and others in a 'neo cross-cultural approach' which, 'Compared to earlier racist material', was 'a much improved approach to Native history', but whose ethnological description 'results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable'.

Readings: Bowsfield (1981); Gagan and Turner (1982); Brown (1983); Pierson (1992, reference list only); LaRocque (1999); McPherson (2000); Fiske (2000). Later readings: Perry (2008); Brown (2012).

nodes.label: Jennifer S. H. Brown
nodes.date_label: Strangers in Blood 1980 · “Woman as Centre and Symbol in the Emergence of Metis Communities” 1983 · The New Peoples (ed. with Peterson) 1985 · The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman) 1988 · “Ethnohistorians: Strange Bedfellows, Kindred Spirits” 1991 · Reading Beyond Words (ed. with Vibert) 1996 · An Ethnohistorian in Rupert’s Land 2017
nodes.description: An anthropologist and historian of fur-trade families, the Métis, and Cree and Ojibwe history in the old Hudson's Bay Company territory. Strangers in Blood (1980) compared Hudson's Bay Company officers and North West Company partners as husbands and fathers; as a 1981 reviewer quoted it, the title took the British legal term for any relationship 'that the law refused to admit as legitimate' as 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians' in the fur trade. In 1983 she asked how women shaped Métis emergence, finding among North West Company fathers who had children baptized in Montreal that daughters were twice as likely as sons to stay in the Indian country, and in 1985 she co-edited with Jacqueline Peterson The New Peoples: Being and Becoming Métis in North America. As president of the American Society for Ethnohistory she spoke of 'our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory' (1991). A 1981 reviewer found the book weighed down by 'bits of anthropological theory'; Emma LaRocque (1999) placed her with Van Kirk in a 'neo cross-cultural approach', 'a much improved approach' on earlier work that still othered its subjects; and later scholarship rejects defining Métis by mixed descent, the biological starting point ('the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups') that her 1983 essay set against a complex social history.

nodes.label: Sherry Olson
nodes.date_label: 'Baltimore Imitates the Spider' 1979 · Baltimore: The Building of an American City 1980 · 'Occupations and Residential Spaces' 1989 · 'Le peuplement de Montréal' 1997 · MAP, Montréal, l'avenir du passé, from 2000 · Peopling the North American City (with Patricia Thornton) 2011 · 'Rebuilding a Neighbourhood of Montreal' (with Dufaux) 2014
nodes.description: A historical geographer, at Johns Hopkins and then McGill, whose Baltimore: The Building of an American City (1980) is 'about city building', read as 'a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks'. In Montreal she and her collaborators, among them the demographer Patricia Thornton, followed sampled families through parish registers, censuses and municipal taxrolls and mapped them; her 1997 chapter for the Atlas historique du Québec, mapped with GIS at McGill, sets out to 'saisir … les processus par lesquels la cité se construit'. With Robert Sweeny, Jason Gilliland and others she built MAP (Montréal, l'avenir du passé, begun in 2000), a collective historical GIS in which, as she and François Dufaux wrote in 2014, 'the spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot'. The editors of Historical GIS Research in Canada (2014) name MAP, 'led by' Olson and Sweeny, among the few Canadian HGIS projects since the 1990s, and a Victoria team that includes Gilliland calls her Montreal work 'a model of spatial history'; Sweeny, MAP's co-director, warned in 2009 that 'the ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding'. With Thornton she wrote Peopling the North American City: Montreal, 1840–1900 (2011), which, by its publisher's description, follows families of twelve surnames.

nodes.scope_note: A method entry for historical GIS, not a Quebec-historiography entry: the Quebec self-accounts read for the atlas (Ouellet 1985, Bédard, Bouchard, Rudin, Savard, Linteau) do not name her. Her own words are read in the introduction and acknowledgments of Baltimore (1980), in full in 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (1997), in part in the 2004 Labour/Le Travail research note, and in part in her 2014 chapter with Dufaux; the 1979, 1998, 2010 and 2011 articles are known from their abstracts, and the 1989 Historical Methods article and the 1990 atlas plate at title level only. Peopling the North American City is unread; it is known from publisher copy and the opening paragraphs of Sager's (2012) and Horner's (2013) reviews. In-period reviews of Baltimore exist (AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture, JEH 1981; JIH, Journal of Historical Geography 1982) but were not readable here. The GIS work begins in the 1990s; MAP dates from 2000 and is collective, co-led with Robert Sweeny, whose team built the electronic framework from the Cane map of 1846. She is not presented as the founder of HGIS in Canada: 'pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, and the editors of the 2014 volume list national repositories in the United States and Britain as 'some of the most important work in the field'. The 2014 volume's chapter 2 (Beard, Macfarlane and Clifford) is not used.

nodes.label: Bruce Curtis
nodes.date_label: With Corrigan, “Education, Inspection and State Formation” 1985 · Building the Educational State 1988 · True Government by Choice Men? 1992 · The Politics of Population 2001 · “After ‘Canada’” 2009 · Ruling by Schooling Quebec 2012
nodes.description: A historical sociologist (Carleton University) whose studies of schooling, school inspection and the census in the Canadas read administration as a means of rule. In Building the Educational State (1988), as a reviewer quotes it, education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (p. 110), and the educational state was built 'only through the destruction of a prior educational organization' (p. 15); in True Government by Choice Men? (1992) 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (p. 32). His census history (2001) holds that 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (p. 305, as Belshaw quotes it), and in a 1996 review he wrote that 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns'. Reviewers credited his joining of Foucault's analysis of power to a Marxist theory of state formation but found gender relations missing (Davey 1989; Miller 1993), and Bryan Palmer judged the inspection study, taken as a model, 'overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (1993). In the debate over Ian McKay's liberal order framework, Nancy Christie cites 'Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality' (2009).

Inspection, Education, and State Formation in Canada West (1992); The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (2001); “After ‘Canada’: Liberalisms, Social Theory, and Historical Analysis” (2009); Ruling by Schooling Quebec: Conquest to Liberal Governmentality – A Historical Sociology (2012).
nodes.scope_note: This entry presents Curtis's state-formation studies of schooling, inspection and the census (1985–2001) and their place in the liberal order debate. Read on 2026-10-14: his review of Darroch and Soltow (1996, pp. 107–110) in full, and four in-period or near-period reviews of his books in full: Davey (1989) on Building the Educational State, Miller (1993) and Palmer (1993) on True Government by Choice Men?, and Belshaw (2002) on The Politics of Population; Christie (2009) was re-read for its Curtis passage. His books are unread: his words from them are reviewers' quotations, with the reviewers' page references. The 1985 article with Corrigan, the 2009 chapter and Ruling by Schooling Quebec (2012) are title- or summary-level only. He is a sociologist, not a historian by department; the atlas's moral regulation entry treats his state-formation work as shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.

nodes.label: Allan Greer
nodes.date_label: “Fur-Trade Labour” 1981 · “A Critique of Pentland” and Peasant, Lord, and Merchant 1985 · Colonial Leviathan (ed. with Radforth) 1992 · The Patriots and the People 1993 · Property and Dispossession 2018 · “Settler Colonialism and Beyond” 2019
nodes.description: A historian of Lower Canada and colonial North America whose rural social history described a feudal, household-centred habitant society: in 1985 he held that Lower Canadian 'agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production', with part of the surplus 'diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions', a view he set against both Ouellet's routine-bound peasant (1981) and the commercial farmer of Paquet and Wallot, while allowing that 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue' (1985). The same essay, a critique of Clare Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, faulted the staples tradition of Innis and Creighton for confining attention to 'relations of exchange'. With Ian Radforth he edited Colonial Leviathan (1992), on mid-nineteenth-century state formation, which Bryan Palmer found to lack coherence (1993) and which Greer later said 'neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (2019); his history of the 1837 rebellion (1993) is known here through reviewers, who read it as breaking with Ouellet's manipulated peasantry. His later work on 'property formation' (2018) and his 2019 lecture treat settler colonialism as one mode of colonial invasion among several, 'a dominant force in some periods and regions' that 'fades to insignificance in others', while insisting 'I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory'.

nodes.label: Cole Harris
nodes.date_label: The Seigneurial System in Early Canada 1966 · Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (editor) 1987 · The Resettlement of British Columbia 1997 · ‘Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia’ 1997–98 · Making Native Space 2002 · ‘Revisiting the Native Land Question’ 2003 · ‘How Did Colonialism Dispossess?’ 2004 · A Bounded Land 2020
nodes.description: A Canadian historical geographer of early Canada and of colonialism in British Columbia. He edited the first volume of the Historical Atlas of Canada (1987), whose preface says it sought 'to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases' (as quoted by MacDonald, 1990). From the 1990s he wrote British Columbia's colonization as geographical change. Against the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era history he set 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (1997–98). He explained the reserve system as dispossession: its capacity 'rested on raw firepower', its momentum 'came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods', and its legitimation 'lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery' (2003); in 2004 he argued that the emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'. Reviewers found few Native voices in the work: Tina Loo (1998) saw Native peoples 'emerge as victims' in The Resettlement of British Columbia, and Val Napoleon (2004) wrote that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and that Harris 'should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices' where history gave way to proposals for the future.

nodes.label: Adele Perry
nodes.date_label: ‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’ 1995 · On the Edge of Empire 2001 · ‘Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History’ 2001 · ‘Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order’ 2009 · Colonial Relations 2015
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of gender, race and colonialism in British Columbia and the British Empire. In 1995 she argued that Canadian historians had explained the shortage of white women in the West with a 'scarcity model' and a 'volcano theory' of male sexuality that were 'based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race' and belonged to 'colonial discourse itself'. On the Edge of Empire (2001), which she said was 'initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism', studied white miners' homosocial culture, mixed-race relationships and the schemes to bring white women to the colony, and found, in her words as reviewers quote them, 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire'. Reviewers placed it in whiteness studies and asked for more on Indigenous people: Sarah Carter (2002) wanted the 'social centrality and political agency' of Aboriginal peoples further developed, and Paul Orlowski (2002) found First Nations resistance 'lacking' and a 'binary racial divide' that set aside Chinese workers. In 2016 she described the 2001 book as arguing that British Columbia's history 'is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Adele Perry; “‘Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men’: Gender Imbalance, Race, Sexuality, and Sociability in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (BC Studies, 1995); “‘Fair Ones of a Purer Caste’: White Women and Colonialism in Nineteenth-Century British Columbia” (1997); “The Historian and the Theorist Revisited” (Histoire sociale/Social History, 2000); On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (2001); “Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History” (BC Studies, 2001/02); “The Autocracy of Love and the Legitimacy of Empire: Intimacy, Power and Scandal in Nineteenth-Century Metlakahtlah” (2004); “Women, Racialized People, and the Making of the Liberal Order in Northern North America” (in Liberalism and Hegemony, 2009); Colonial Relations: The Douglas-Connolly Family and the Nineteenth-Century Imperial World (2015). Readings: Carter (2002); Orlowski (2002); Rutherdale (2002); the BC Studies forum on Colonial Relations (Clayton, Dussart, Devine, Ballantyne, 2016).
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14 in open copies. Her own words, read: '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”' (BC Studies 105/106, 1995, pp. 27–44; pp. 27–33 and 42–43 read closely, the middle skimmed); 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History' (BC Studies 132, 2001/02, pp. 57–64, read in full); her reply in the BC Studies forum on Colonial Relations (190, 2016, pp. 106–114, read at pp. 106–108 and 112–113; a later reading). Reviews of On the Edge of Empire read in full: Sarah Carter (BC Studies 136, 2002/03, pp. 117–119); Paul Orlowski (Left History 8:1, 2002, pp. 119–122, in an Internet Archive capture, since the York journal site serves a browser check); Myra Rutherdale (Labour/Le Travail 50, 2002, pp. 324–326). Later reading: Tony Ballantyne in the 2016 forum (pp. 104–105). Unread: On the Edge of Empire itself (quoted only through its reviewers, with their page references), 'Fair Ones of a Purer Caste' (1997), 'The Historian and the Theorist Revisited' (Histoire sociale 2000; York site behind a browser check), the 2009 liberal-order chapter (title level), Colonial Relations (2015) and the other 2016 forum reviews except as noted. A search engine's summary first attributed the Left History review to Greg Dening; the PDF shows it is Paul Orlowski's (Dening reviewed the preceding book). Contested in period by Carter (2002) and Orlowski (2002) on Indigenous agency, by Orlowski on class and the omission of Chinese workers, and by Rutherdale (2002) on the metropolitan side; in 1995 she said her own analysis 'minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text.

edges.relationship: Workers' control and class at the centre: Toronto skilled workers' power on the job (1976) and their responses to industrial capitalism (1980), with a periodization by stages of capitalism and a case for class analysis and the materiality of culture (1978–81); contested by Bercuson and Brody (1981) and by feminist critics (1987–2000)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. '“The Honest Workingman” and Workers’ Control', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 32–68, read at pp. 32–34 and 58–62: 'Skilled workers in the nineteenth century exercised far more power than we have previously realized. … In Toronto work places, craftsmen employed their monopoly on skill and experience to dictate terms to their employers … which, in modern parlance, gave to these late nineteenth century craftsmen a high degree of workers' control of production' (p. 32); he draws on David Montgomery's 'veterans of industrial life' and on Raymond Williams's 'residual' and 'emergent' (p. 33); 'The custom of workers' control, widely regarded as a right, had become deeply embedded in working class culture' and its defence 'became the major locus of class struggle in the opening decades of the twentieth century' (p. 62). 'The Working Class in Recent Canadian Historical Writing', Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), pp. 116–135, read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: historians still treat the new study of class 'as little more than interesting additional facts', but 'the new history is well on its way to transforming our understanding of the entire course and structure of Canadian development' (p. 116). 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 67–94, read in full: the project 'never excluded the study of unions and labour politics', nor called for history 'simply "written from the bottom up," since it always placed the relationship between classes at the centre of the story' (p. 69); a periodization of 'pre-industrial capitalism to 1850; industrial capitalism, 1850 to the mid-1890s; monopoly capitalism, 1890s to 1929; and crisis and reconstruction, 1930 to the present', offered as 'at best tentative' (p. 74); 'I will certainly stand with scholars such as Thompson and Williams who have argued persuasively for the materiality of culture itself' (p. 85); class 'does have an "objective" side', but '"Class-for-itself," or the failure of the working class to develop such, is almost by definition what working-class history concerns itself with' (pp. 85–86); work on the 1880s found 'a class surprisingly united', in which divisions 'of ethnicity, skill, religion, and even sex were recognized, debated, and for a few years in the 1880s, at least, were overcome', and 'it is now necessary to locate class conflict and class struggle at the centre of modern Canadian history' (p. 89). He places himself among scholars who were 'active in the new left and influenced by the rebirth of Marxist scholarship' (p. 93). Toronto Workers (1980) is unread; Brody quotes its introduction: 'The work will have succeeded to the extent that it provides convincing evidence that the working class was not just "made" but rather was the result of a dialectical interplay of class forces in which it was one of the actors' (p. xviii, as quoted). In-period critics. David Bercuson, in the same issue (pp. 95–96, read), quotes the 1976 Essays definition of the new labour history and notes that 'Kealey's study of Toronto workers contains at least five chapters devoted to working-class and trade-union politics'; his wider objections are recorded under wcreq_bercuson_1981 and edge_919. David Brody, review, Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), pp. 361–364, read in full: 'Kealey thus lays the foundation, hitherto largely lacking, for a history of the Toronto labour movement' (p. 362), but 'It is in the interpretation of this information that the book founders'; 'Every strike signifies "class conflict," every labour involvement in public life "class politics"' (p. 363); 'Having overreached himself, he has produced only a useable one' (p. 364). Ian McKay, 'Historians, Anthropology, and the Concept of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9 (1981–82), cites Kealey's 1981 'defence of the term' (p. 214 n. 88) and argues that working-class culture has 'weak explanatory value' and that Williams's residual and emergent categories 'merely have allowed social historians to indulge in retrospective cheerleading for progressive ideas' (p. 223 and n. 122); Kealey in 1981 called McKay's unpublished paper 'one of the most substantive critiques of Thompson and culturalism' (p. 91 n.). Bettina Bradbury (1987, pp. 35–36, read) and Joan Sangster (2000, p. 133, read): see edge pe138_kealey_rel_05 and the node; Sangster: 'One of the first major collections of the new labour history contained not one article on women' (p. 133, of Kealey and Warrian's Essays, 1976). Desmond Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; 'If, as Kealey insisted, Toronto's working class achieved unity across ethnic and sectarian barriers, it must have been for the briefest of moments in the city contemporaries sometimes called "the Belfast of North America"'. A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names him in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail; he presents the work as 'conceived collectively' (1981, p. 68 n. 8). Scope: this edge is Kealey's own contribution; edge_919 carries Palmer's craft culture, edge_886 and edge_890 the Marxist and Thompsonian resources. The Knights of Labor book (1982) is unread and appears in pe138_kealey_rel_05.

edges.relationship: Limited identities and regional explanation criticised from a class standpoint: 'limited identities' as 'neither "limited" nor analytically separable' (1978), region as 'the crucial variable' 'increasingly misplaced' and western exceptionalism overstated (1981), and the 1919 revolt as 'national in character' (1984)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. Acadiensis 7:2 (1978), read at pp. 116–117 and 134–135: Cook and Careless 'called for a turn away from nation and politics' toward 'region, ethnicity and class' (p. 116, citing Cook 1967 and Careless 1969); 'The call for attention to "limited identities" was the death-knell of Laurentianism' (p. 117); 'The long-overdue insertion of a class analysis into Canadian historical writing already promises overviews which transcend the refreshing and liberating pluralism of the 1960s calls for attention to region, ethnicity and class. It should be increasingly clear, however, that these so-called "limited identities" are neither "limited" nor analytically separable. No historical notion of class (and there can be no other useful notion) can fail to incorporate ethnicity and place' (p. 135). Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), read in full: 'NONE CAN DENY the importance of regional differences … Yet the increasing emphasis placed on "region" as the crucial variable which explains sundry problems of Canadian development seems increasingly misplaced', citing Westfall on the regional interpretation standing 'the old nationalist history on its head' (p. 74); before the 1890s 'there was not one Canadian working class but many' (p. 75); accounts of western workers are shaped by 'a strong sense of western exceptionalism', and 'the rather easy assumptions of a unique western working-class militancy have been overstated', with n. 25: 'David Bercuson has been most guilty of this' (p. 76); 'Canadian historians have come to believe everything was different everywhere … This celebration of region has fit very well with the general direction of Canadian political life in the last decade. Surely the time has come to begin to reflect on region in a critical way' (p. 76); his remedy is not 'A return to an old national history? No, of course not, but rather the consideration on a national scale of the particular class experiences of Canadian workers in local and regional contexts which adds up to something more than local and regional exceptionalism' (p. 77). '1919: The Canadian Labour Revolt', Labour/Le Travail 13 (1984), pp. 11–44, read at pp. 11–17: 'These examples are intended simply to demonstrate that the revolt was national in character and that its seeds were not rooted in any unique regional fermentation. The "radical" west and the conservative east have become sorry shibboleths of Canadian historiography'; 'the similarities of struggle begin to outweigh the initial impression of regional particularism' (p. 15). Qualifications kept: he grants 'the importance of regional differences' (1981, p. 74) and calls Maritime underdevelopment real (pp. 75–76); the 1978 sentence welcomes the 1960s pluralism as 'refreshing and liberating' before arguing that class analysis transcends it. In-period reading: Morton (2000, p. 25, read) credits Kealey, Palmer, Heron, Hann and others with bringing labour history 'back from superstructure, politics, and the exceptionalism of Western Canada to regions that had been largely neglected by their predecessors: Ontario and the Maritimes'. No reply by Bercuson to the 1981 or 1984 regional argument was checked. Distinct from Cook's 1977–83 critique of regionalism (edge from ramsay_cook to cdn_regional), which doubts region as a unit; Kealey's subordinates it to class and national-scale capitalism.

edges.relationship: Herbert Gutman's cultural history of American workers and David Montgomery's workers' control as models for Kealey's Toronto studies (1976–81), as Kealey and his reviewers said, with the criticisms of Gutman he reported and Brody's verdict that he did not follow Gutman's method
edges.evidence_note: His own statements. 1976 (Labour/Le Travailleur 1, read at pp. 32–34, 58): 'David Montgomery has suggested that we must look beyond pre-industrial cultural forms if we are to understand the behaviour of skilled workers', who were 'veterans of industrial life' (p. 33); on the meaning of shop-floor power, 'David Montgomery has argued that the major impact of this early workers' control was the skilled workers' growing awareness that the key institution for the transformation of society was the trade union' (p. 58). 1978 (Acadiensis, p. 117): the works of Thompson and Hobsbawm, 'and later of Americans such as Herbert Gutman and David Montgomery, had their effects in Canada on a new generation of graduate students'. 1981 (Labour/Le Travailleur 7, read in full): 'A cultural approach in American work on labour history also generated a significant breakthrough. Most notably associated with Herbert Gutman' (p. 81); n. 33: 'Gutman's influence can be seen in numerous recent studies. In Canada see Palmer, A Culture in Conflict and Kealey, Toronto Workers' (p. 82). He reports Dubofsky's and Montgomery's worry about 'the failure to consider the political and economic context' and Brody's charge that Gutman 'shifted the Thompsonian focus on class and culture into a focus solely on culture' (pp. 81–82). In-period readers. David Brody (Labour/Le Travailleur 8/9, 1981–82, read): 'During his tenure at Rochester a decade or so ago, Herbert G. Gutman built up a remarkable graduate program in American working-class history … Gregory Kealey's book bears the marks of what might be termed the Gutman school' (p. 361); but 'In one crucial way, unfortunately, it does not': Gutman 'invariably has drawn his ideas out from the evidence', and 'Had he adhered to the prudent craft of his mentor, Kealey might have written a powerful book' (p. 364). Morton (2000, pp. 22–23, read): the 'second generation' 'travelled abroad, to Warwick, Rochester, and Binghamton, to meet their American and British mentors', and the Knights of Labor records 'Kealey had been able to study at Rochester'. Later engagement, title level only: 'Herbert G. Gutman, 1928–1985, and the Writing of Working-Class History' (Monthly Review, 1986) and 'Gutman and Montgomery' (ILWCH, 1990; wcreq_kealey_1990). Gutman and Montgomery are historians on the newleft roster (work_cultures strand). Influence, not discipleship: the 1981 essay also gives Thompson and Williams as touchstones, and edge_890 carries Thompson's place in the field. edge_888 (newleft ↔ cdn_working_class) stays as the group-level comparison.

edges.relationship: State surveillance of labour and the left from the First World War: a 1992 documentary article on the RCMP and the Special Branch, arguing that 'For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946', and the RCMP Security Bulletins he co-edited with Whitaker (1989–97); the work was announced as under way in 1988, and the later syntheses Secret Service (2012, with Whitaker and Parnaby) and Spying on Canadians (2017) are cited at catalogue level only
edges.evidence_note: The checked intervention, 1992. 'The RCMP, the Special Branch, and the Early Days of the Communist Party of Canada: A Documentary Article', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 169–204, introduction read (pp. 169–171; the documents themselves not read): a 1991 visit to the Public Record Office in London, 'when combined with a number of Access to Information requests to the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS), provides considerable insight into the early co-operation between the fledgling Royal Canadian Mounted Police security and intelligence apparatus of the early 1920s and its more experienced partners in England' (p. 169); the weekly RCMP security bulletin was 'circulated to Cabinet', and the bulletins were 'routinely sent to the Special Branch at the Colonial Office' (p. 170); 'Such documentation also makes clear how early Canadian intelligence efforts focused on labour radicalism and socialism. For the RCMP the Cold War began in 1919, not in 1946' (p. 171). His n. 4 (p. 170) describes 'the multi-volume Gregory S. Kealey and Reg Whitaker, eds., The RCMP Security Bulletins (St. John's 1989 and forthcoming)', drawn 'primarily' from Access requests to CSIS; the edition itself is known only through that note and review records. Earlier notice, not a checked argument: the 1988 author note in Class, Gender, and Region (p. iv, read) says only that he 'is currently working on Canadian state repression of labour and the left'; the 1919 essay (1984, p. 43, read) draws on an RCMP draft memorandum of September 1919. Later works, catalogue level only and not assessed here: 'State Repression of Labour and the Left in Canada, 1914–20' (CHR 73:3, 1992, pp. 281–314) and 'The Surveillance State' (Intelligence and National Security 7:3, 1992, pp. 179–210), both reprinted as chapters of Spying on Canadians (2017; UTP chapter records); Secret Service: Political Policing in Canada from the Fenians to Fortress America (2012), by Reg Whitaker, Gregory S. Kealey and Andrew Parnaby (publisher's description: 'the many tensions that arise when undercover police and their covert methods are deployed too freely in a liberal democratic society'). The edge therefore claims the 1992 argument and the edition, not the content of the later syntheses. Relation to the strand: security_state currently holds Whitaker and Marcuse's Cold War Canada (1945–57). Kealey's argument dates the security state's anti-communist focus to 1919; this is an extension in time by Whitaker's co-editor, not a critique of their book. No in-period reviews of the Bulletins were read (Dansereau, RHAF 1995, located only).
