edges.relationship: Co-authors of Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and allies in the new labour history, read together by critics as 'the Kealey-Palmer claims', though 'differently positioned politically' (Sangster) and with different emphases: workers' control and class analysis for Kealey, craft culture for Palmer
edges.evidence_note: Collaboration, in their own texts. Kealey's 1976 essay thanks Palmer, with David Frank and Craig Heron, for comments (p. 32 n.); the 1981 essay thanks him among others (p. 94), refers readers to Palmer's forthcoming Making of E.P. Thompson (p. 82), and says that 'Kealey and Palmer, "Dreaming of What Might Be"' 'argues this position at length' on the value of the romantic and utopian traditions, which gave workers 'the ability to dream of an alternative future' (p. 84 and n. 39). Read together by critics, in period. Bercuson (1981, p. 96): 'the Palmer and Kealey books' as 'restricted but intensive studies'. Bradbury (Labour/Le Travail 19, 1987, pp. 35–36, read) quotes Dreaming (p. 318) and writes that to dismiss partially a Knights of Labor editor's picture of a wife who 'can darn a stocking' 'as "offensive" and as "crude moralizing," as Kealey and Palmer do, seems to me both to deny the realities of the division of labour within the working-class family economy at that time, and to close off the possibility of examining this very important element of a skilled worker's pride'; she adds that 'Kealey and Palmer quite rightly point out' that a Montreal workman's statement stopped short of a critique of 'women's proper sphere'. Sangster (Labour/Le Travail 46, 2000, p. 133, read): 'Two seminal studies followed by Gregory Kealey and Bryan Palmer. Though differently positioned politically, they examined workers' responses to 19th century industrialization, with a proclivity to centre on skilled male workers and their actions in the public sphere.' Morton (2000, pp. 23–24, read): 'some of the Kealey-Palmer claims for their "new" history were challenged'; Stanley Ryerson (1981, as Morton reports it) argued that the Knights were 'devoutly committed to labour-employer harmony and industrial peace'. Later reading, labelled: McCoy (2021) quotes their chapter: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). The book itself is unread. A comparison, not an influence: the edge records co-authorship and joint reception. Their different emphases are recorded in edge_919 (Palmer's craft culture) and pe138_kealey_rel_01 (Kealey's workers' control and class analysis).

edges.relationship: Careless's second thoughts about the 'flood' of regional, cultural and class writing (1979 lecture) read as a reaction reasserting 'a "positive" unifying national history' (1988); a decade earlier the working-class bibliography Kealey co-compiled had invoked Careless's limited identities (1973)
edges.evidence_note: Kealey's words, in period. Introduction to Class, Gender, and Region: Essays in Canadian Historical Sociology (St. John's: CCLH, 1988; reprint of a Canadian Journal of Sociology special issue), pp. 1–7, read in the AU Press PDF: 'The degree to which reaction has re-emerged to reassert the need for a "positive" unifying national history can be seen by contrasting the views of J.M.S. Careless in 1969 and in 1980. In 1969, Careless enthusiastically embraced Ramsay Cook's earlier call for the study of region, class, and ethnicity … By 1980, however, he had serious doubts' (p. 2); he quotes Careless's farmer 'in the midst of the flood' and answers: 'As I hope this volume suggests, such plaintiff [sic] Toronto cries to date have not been able to dam the flood of critical scholarship on class, gender, and region' (p. 3). 'The impatience mentioned by Berger and articulated by Careless addresses itself as much to this regional revolt as it does to writings concerned with class and gender' (p. 5). Careless's text, re-read (Manitoba History no. 1, web text, unpaginated; the 1979 Jackson lecture, cited by Kealey as 1980): 'there has been a massive outpouring … on class disparities and stresses and such things as national concerns are by and large passed over or discounted. In this situation, I feel a little like the farmer in the midst of a flood'. Qualifications kept: Careless continues, 'there are reasons why I do not really feel as bad as the foregoing might suggest', calls working-class history 'one of the most active and productive areas' of the study of limited identities, and asks that class identities 'be treated in their national scope', a point close to Kealey's own (1981, p. 77). Kealey's 'reaction' is his reading of the lecture. Earlier connection: Careless (1979) quotes the introduction to Primary Sources in Canadian Working-Class History (1973, p. 11), compiled by Hann, Gregory and Linda Kealey and Warrian: 'For some time J. M. S. Careless has called for … a historical appreciation of the varieties of "limited identities" that constitute Canada'. Kealey (1981, p. 68) says that statement was 'drafted by Russell Hann'. No reply by Careless was checked. Related: edge_954 (Careless → who_killed_debate) records the fragmentation worry this passage voices; pe138_kealey_rel_02 records Kealey's separate critique of limited identities from a class standpoint (1978).

edges.relationship: Ethnic history criticised for treating ethnicity apart from class and for 'official ethnic interpreters' whose celebratory histories leave out working-class militancy, while ethnicity is kept as a subject of cultural analysis (1981)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period: 'Labour and Working-Class History in Canada: Prospects in the 1980s', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), section III, 'Ethnicity', pp. 77–80, read in full. 'The literature on ethnicity and immigration, even in "multicultural" Canada, too often ignores ethnicity as an ongoing factor in historical analysis. … Instead one might question the official ethnic interpreters of their history where middle class bias and, all too often, cold war assumptions have come to dominate the quasi-official version of the past. This past, which celebrates the achievements of each ethnic community, has little room in its pages for the embarrassments of working-class militancy and radical politics' (p. 78); 'Ethnicity considered independent of class often obscures important issues', with the Italian padrone 'King' Cordasco as an instance of 'important class divisions within the ethnic communities themselves'; 'Here again class will prove more crucial than some ethnic historians have previously suggested' (p. 79). He also notes that labour historians who studied militancy (Bercuson, McCormack, Abella) 'have moved towards ethnicity as a crucial variable for further study' (p. 88). Qualifications kept: 'Concern for the ethnic divisions within the working class then is important and valid' (p. 73); 'This qualification is not meant to diminish the significance of ethnicity and of the potentially divisive nature of ethnic heterogeneity to the Canadian working class' (p. 78); ethnicity 'is one of the major areas which demands a cultural analysis' (p. 77), and 'cultural analysis will be central to this project' (p. 80). He cites Avery's 'Dangerous Foreigners' (1979) and Harney on padronism in his notes (p. 79). Scope: a critique of ethnic history that sets ethnicity apart from class and of community-sponsored celebratory history, not of the immigrant-workers literature (Avery) the entry's workers_radicalism strand holds. Perin's 'Clio as an Ethnic' (1983) in the ethnic_history_debate strand is a separate, later critique; no exchange between them was checked.

edges.relationship: Women and marriage à la façon du pays at the centre of fur-trade society, and missionary racism against Native wives in Red River (1980–86)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. 'Many Tender Ties' (1980) is unread here and is quoted only as Bowsfield quotes it (Archivaria 12, 1981, review article, read in full; he gives no page references to the book). He reports her purpose as showing that the fur trade 'constituted a social and cultural complex as well as an economic activity'. He quotes her claims that 'If a man formed a liaison with a woman she was considered to be his wife, entitled to the recognition and support that a marital relationship implied' and that Indian women's work 'constituted an important contribution to the functioning of the trade'. He paraphrases her account of a marriage rite à la façon du pays and of the later turn from Indian to mixed-descent and then white wives, as younger officers became 'imbued with the Victorian middle-class desire for respectability and success' (p. 124). Gagan and Turner (Archivaria 14, 1982, read in full) summarise her argument that these marriages, 'generations of scandalized references notwithstanding, were crucial to the establishment of early western society' (p. 43). Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, web edition, read in full; no page numbers): 'Fur trade society in Rupert's Land had resulted from decades of inter-marriage among incoming white fur traders with Indian and later mixed-blood women'; 'Racist attitudes, particularly with regard to women, can be seen in the attempts of the missionaries to enforce their concepts of morality upon a society that had developed its own indigenous customs.' Brown (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full) takes 'the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) on the socioeconomic role of women in the fur trade' as one starting point for Métis history (p. 40). Criticism: Bowsfield notes her view that such unions were not 'casual' or 'promiscuous' and comments, 'This may be too complimentary a picture of both native women and European men' (p. 124). LaRocque's criticism (1999) is recorded on pe139_vankirk_rel_04, and edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques at entry level. Not a founding: Bowsfield reviews the book within a fur-trade literature already recast by Ray, Trigger and others (pp. 121–24). Later reading, labelled: Perry (Left History 13:2, 2008, read in full) writes that 'In the early 1990s Van Kirk's work particularly garnered some sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques, ones that made clear how wedded "Many Tender Ties" was to a Eurocentric, celebratory sort of liberal feminism', and then that Van Kirk's and Brown's 'symbiotic arguments about the centrality of women and family to the Canadian fur-trade' have 'never been cast into serious doubt' (p. 163). The critiques she cites (n. 7: Pierson 1992; Emberley 1990–91) are unread here.

edges.relationship: Indigenous and mixed-descent women written into Canadian women's history, with race as a division among women (1980–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. As Bowsfield quotes the book (Archivaria 12, 1981, p. 124; no page given), Van Kirk claimed that it 'supports the claims of theorists in women's history that sex roles should constitute a category of historical investigation', and she admitted the limits of relying on male sources. He finds 'a feminist note to some of Van Kirk's statements but it must be admitted that it is not a strident one'. Gagan and Turner's survey of Canadian social history (Archivaria 14, 1982, p. 29 and n. 7) puts 'Many Tender Ties' and Strangers in Blood under women's work: 'two noteworthy recent studies attempt to recreate the whole way of life of a particular group of "working" women, those who participated in the Canadian fur trade', in which 'the whole woman-wife, mother, labourer, diplomat, chattel, entrepreneur-is revealed'. Her own words, 1986 (Manitoba History 11, read in full): 'Other important themes for women's history also emerge'; 'The reasons for such "unsisterly" action should be confronted squarely by feminist historians'; 'The rivalry among women in nineteenth century Red River, however, was compounded by the issue of race'; and 'The racism evinced by white women in Red River, while as inexcusable as that of their male counterparts, was aggravated by what, in their view, was a concrete threat to their own welfare in the competition for eligible husbands.' 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, pp. 149–51 read): 'Little attention has been paid to the fact that this process of acculturation was gendered'; 'a complex interaction of gender and class dynamics, coupled with the particular demographics of early Victoria, enabled the girls to transcend the racist climate of the colony more successfully than the boys' (p. 150). Reception in a Canadian women's studies journal, 2000 (Atlantis 25:1, both read in full): McPherson calls the book a 'now-classic work' and writes that 'Van Kirk's research and the critical debates it has aroused have played a crucial role in writing Native women into western Canadian history and in bringing cultural difference and conflict into Canadian women's history' (p. 82). Fiske writes that understanding the discursive formation of Aboriginal women's sexuality 'requires us to build on the early work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) and Jennifer Brown (1980) by placing Aboriginal women in the context of the expectations held of settler women' (p. 12); this extends the work rather than rejecting it. Pierson's 'Colonization and Canadian Women's History' (1992) cites the book (OpenAlex reference list only; text unread). Criticism is recorded on rel_01 (Bowsfield) and rel_04 (LaRocque). edge_872 compares the two field entries at title level; this edge adds her own words and the field's reading of her.

edges.relationship: Two 1980 studies of fur-trade marriage and family, read as a pair: women and marriage (Van Kirk) and company officers' families and descent (Brown)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981, read in full) reviews the books together: 'In Strangers in Blood Jennifer Brown, using basically the same sources and employing the same macrobiographical approach as Van Kirk, examines the fur traders group looking at their social background, their domestic lives, their family relationships, and the fate of their children'. He singles out Brown's 'comparison between Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company men as husbands and fathers' (p. 124). He concludes: 'With Van Kirk and Brown the unique and complex role of women and the fur trade family unit have been opened to investigation', and 'Through the study of fur trade families a distinctive Canadian approach to family history has been developed' (p. 126). Gagan and Turner (1982, p. 29, n. 7) cite the two books in one note as studies of working women. Brown (CJNS, 1983, read in full) builds on both books. 'Another starting point for this discussion is the work of Sylvia Van Kirk (1980) on the socioeconomic role of women in the fur trade' (p. 40); 'A third incentive for writing this paper comes from pursuing the implications of what I have called the patrifocality that characterized some upper-level fur trade families' (p. 41). Their own in-period words differ in frame. Van Kirk writes of 'themes for women's history' and of what 'feminist historians' should confront, among women divided by race in Red River (1986). Brown uses the anthropological models of 'matriorganization' and 'unilocality' to ask how women and descent shaped 'metis emergence' (1983, pp. 40–42). LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249) criticises both in one list. Later readings, labelled. Brown (2012, read in the 2017 reprint) recalls: 'We became, it seemed, the Bobbsey Twins of fur trade social history, often cited in the same breath or footnote by writers who might or might not have read our books' (p. 187). She also says that 'her sphere of work and teaching increasingly became women's history, while mine focused more on Aboriginal history' (p. 191), and that Van Kirk 'tended to accept more as given' categories such as 'marriage,' 'custom,' and 'society' (pp. 191–92). Van Kirk 'had a devotion to the ones that worked', whereas 'my book title, Strangers in Blood, picked up on a different angle' (p. 192). Brown quotes Van Kirk's letter of 1972: 'As an anthropologist you will likely be applying a different set of criteria to the primary source material' (p. 184); the letter is known here only through that 2012 quotation. Perry (2008) writes that 'Brown's analysis placed family and kinship at the centre of fur-trade life, and Van Kirk's argued for the centrality of women' (p. 162), and calls their arguments 'symbiotic' (p. 163). This is a comparison, and no direction is asserted. Each person's contribution sits on her own edges to native_newcomer.

edges.relationship: LaRocque: cross-cultural ethnological description of Native and Métis women as othering, 1999
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Emma LaRocque's specified criticism in her 1999 University of Manitoba dissertation (read at PDF pp. 54 and 249), not a verdict of the Indigenous history entry. She describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)', which 'tended to frame all things Native in typical terms of "cultural differences" or "traditions."' She grants: 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history. And with greater awareness, there is greater improvement.' But 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect', and 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience' (p. 249). Her note 18 names the book: 'See in Many Tender Ties, for example, Van Kirk's listing of all the items of fashion or jewelry metis women were "very fond of" (101-103). There is an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable" for these women to acquire' (p. 249, n. 18). In an earlier note she cites the book, with Saum and Ray and Freeman, among fur-trade studies that record Native resistance (PDF p. 54, note). Brown is named in the same list on p. 249 and the criticism is noted on her own entry (pe139_brown_rel_01); one arrow is drawn, to Van Kirk, because the note's example is hers. edge_868 (indigenous → native_newcomer) already carries LaRocque with Sioui and Stevenson (Wheeler) at entry level; this edge records the person-level target. OCR slips in the PDF text layer are corrected ('Van Krk', 'al1', 'hrterests'). The page numbers are PDF pages, as in edge_868. No identity classification is recorded. Later reading, labelled: Perry (2008, p. 163) dates 'sharp post-colonial, anti-racist, and post-structuralist critiques' of Van Kirk's work to the early 1990s; those texts are unread here.

edges.relationship: Company families compared, and women and descent in Métis emergence: Hudson's Bay and North West Company fathers, mothers and children (1980–85)
edges.evidence_note: In-period. Strangers in Blood (1980) is unread here. Gresko (Canadian Woman Studies 3:2, 1981, read in full) quotes the book's double sense of its title: the British legal term for 'any relationship, even familial that the law refused to admit as legitimate', and 'one way of characterizing the meetings of Whites and Indians ... in the fur trade of North America'. She reports that before 1821 the two companies, despite 'their common British (and heavily Scottish) facade', built different social organisations in Indian country. She quotes Brown that later social distinctions were 'strongly related to changing economic pressures' and that old Nor'Westers tended 'not to assume an active paternal role' (pp. 112–13). Bowsfield (Archivaria 12, 1981) singles out the 'comparison between Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company men as husbands and fathers', which Brown relates partly to 'the relationship of hinterland to metropolis' (p. 124). Her own words come from a paper to the Métis symposium held in Winnipeg in November 1982 (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, 1983, read in full). 'Biologically, métissage in North America can be described in a unitary way, as the meeting and mingling of Indian and white racial groups. Socially and culturally, it has had a complex history over many generations' (p. 40). Among Nor'Westers who had children baptized in Montreal, 1796–1821, sons were favoured 'by a margin of about two to one', so daughters 'were more likely by a two-to-one margin to remain in the Indian country, marrying there and contributing to the very rapid growth of biracial population' (p. 41). Coltman, Pambrun and McGillivray in 1818 'were all in accord in calling attention to the maternal element as formative in metis emergence' (p. 44). 'It is all too easy to learn more about the men than the women' (p. 45). The essay cites The New Peoples, then forthcoming from the 1981 Newberry Library Conference on the Metis; the 1985 collection itself is title-level here. Criticism. Gresko finds the book 'still too much in the form of the academic thesis' and 'complicated by seemingly insignificant bits of anthropological theory', and notes that it does not mention Jamieson's Indian Women and the Law in Canada (1978) (p. 113). LaRocque (1999, PDF p. 249) names Brown in the 'neo cross-cultural approach' that she criticises (see pe139_vankirk_rel_04 and edge_868). Not a founding: in 1983 she places her questions beside Jacqueline Peterson's (1981, 1982) and Van Kirk's (1980) (p. 40). Later readings, labelled. Gaudry (aboriginal policy studies 2:2, 2013, read in full) uses Peterson and Brown (1985) for the distinction between 'small-m métis', 'mixed Indigenous and European from a diversity of backgrounds', and 'big-M Métis', 'descended from the Red River Métis people, the New Nation'. With Andersen (2011, as Gaudry quotes him; unread), he rejects reducing 'the astonishing complexity of Red River Métis to their ostensible mixedness' (p. 78). He does not attribute that reduction to Peterson and Brown. In the 2017 reprint of her 1985 essay, Brown drops 'Presbyterian Métis' from the title. 'The term "Métis," as used in Rupert's Land in the 1800s, referred particularly to Roman Catholics of French Canadian paternal origin', and the children 'cannot be subsumed under any one label' (pp. 145–46).

edges.relationship: Anthropological models brought to fur-trade, court and mission records for Métis, Cree and Ojibwe history (1983–96)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. The 1983 essay (Canadian Journal of Native Studies 3:1, read in full) reads fur-trade sources through anthropological models. Bishop and Krech's argument for early subarctic 'matriorganization' leads her to ask 'whether native women in emergent metis groups looked for and found ways to maintain this organizational bias in their own families and social lives' (p. 40). She tests Asch's 'unilocality' among the Slavey against fur-trade families (p. 42), using the HBC district report on Île-à-la-Crosse of 1823 (p. 42) and the published Red River testimonies of 1818 (pp. 43–44). She presents women's studies as 'one important perspective, among several' (p. 40). Her presidential address to the American Society for Ethnohistory (Ethnohistory 38:2, 1991) is known through an indexed excerpt only, OpenAlex's abstract field; the page itself was not inspected. It speaks of 'the rather obscure niche occupied by our field, methodology, approach, or whatever it is we do when we do ethnohistory', and offers 'auto-ethnohistory' as 'a useful handle for some reflections about ethnohistory and ethnohistorians, myself included' (indexed excerpt; p. 113 is the recorded first page). Title-level: The Orders of the Dreamed (with Brightman, 1988), an edition of the trader George Nelson's 1823 account of Cree and Northern Ojibwa religion and myth, and Reading Beyond Words: Contexts for Native History (ed. with Vibert, 1996). Reception, read in full: Fiske (Atlantis 25:1, 2000) cites Brown and Vibert (1996) for the literary turn 'that subjects both oral and written narratives to textual analysis' (p. 13). McPherson (2000, n. 31) cites an essay in that volume as discursive analysis of a Red River trial. Gresko (1981) objected to the 'bits of anthropological theory' in Strangers in Blood (p. 113). Later readings, labelled. Brown (2012, read in the 2017 reprint) recalls that 'my courses and professors directed me towards broader issues of method and theory'. She also says she 'benefited from confronting the multiple problems around defining such categories as "marriage," "custom," and "society"' (pp. 191–92). The 2017 part introduction calls the pair 'I coming from anthropology and Sylvia from history' (p. 159). Her essay 'The Blind Men and the Elephant' (1990) is read only in its revised 2017 reprint, which cites a 2014 book. There she asks historians to 'start by deconstructing' the fur trade, and warns that subsuming northern Native history under 'the fur trade era' restricts it to 'certain rather specialized "Indian-White relations"' (pp. 63–65); the 1990 wording is unchecked. The edge claims a contribution to the field's documentary method, not that she shaped ethnohistory as a whole.

edges.relationship: Households placed on the urban lot: linked parish, census and tax records for nineteenth-century Montreal, mapped with GIS at McGill in the 1990s and built from 2000 into the collective MAP geodatabase
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. 'Le peuplement de Montréal' (Atlas historique du Québec, 1997; read in full) works from 'l’exemple local pour ensuite faire ressortir la vue d’ensemble et saisir ainsi, dans une démarche exploratoire, les processus par lesquels la cité se construit' (p. 81). Its samples are built from records, and differ by population: the Catholic baptismal cohort of 1859, whose parents were traced through the Drouin index and the Notre-Dame registers (n. 4); for the Protestant population only, a micro-sample of ten surnames ('Pour la population protestante, notre microéchantillon s’appuie sur dix patronymes', p. 85), distinct from the twelve-surname sampling that the publisher's description gives for the later book with Thornton (2011, unread here); a 'Montréal « miniaturisé »' of 370 household heads in 1900, and building tradesmen from the 'rôle d’évaluation' plotted in half-kilometre rings 'à la manière d’une reconstitution cinématographique' (p. 89). Note 1 credits the demographic analysis to Patricia Thornton and the mapping 'sur ATLAS GIS' to Ben Johnson and Ingrid Olson, with the McGill GIS laboratory. Earlier work is known only at title level ('Occupations and Residential Spaces', Historical Methods, 1989) or from an abstract (with Gilliland, Urban History Review, 1998: 'From small samples of the Montreal population over the years 1861-1901'). After 2000, her own words. In 2004 she describes the method and its limits: cross-referencing the 1842 census, the 1848 directory and the 1848 taxroll 'in an iterative process of matching surnames, first names, streets of residence, and occupations'; of 5,192 taxroll entries '75 per cent can be matched to the directory, 45 per cent to the census 5 years earlier, and 41 per cent to both sources' (Labour/Le Travail 53, pp. 173–74). In the same note Robert Sweeny 'has created from the Cane map an electronic framework' (p. 165, note). With Dufaux (2014): MAP is 'a collective project in which dozens of people have invested their skills'; 'The spatial links place the household on the cadastral lot – 7,000 lots in the 1850s, 30,000 in 1900' (p. 155); 'A dozen Montreal scholars and a dozen graduate students initiated the project in 2000' (p. 176 n. 1). From abstracts: the 2010 and 2011 papers with Gilliland (and Gauvreau) locate '17,000 individual households' in 1881 and re-aggregate lots into 'districts with identical boundaries for both years', 'overcoming the major methodological problems hindering previous comparative analyses'. Reception (later readings, labelled). Bonnell and Fortin (2014, p. xii): 'Since the 1990s, only a small number of historical geographers and historians have used GIS technology' in Canada; 'Notable projects include Montréal, l’avenir du passé, a comprehensive HGIS database of Montreal led by McGill geographer Sherry Olson and Memorial University historian Robert Sweeny'; 'Olson, Sweeny, and Gilliland’s work has captured the interest of a new generation of graduate students and new scholars' (p. xiii). Lutz, Dunae, Gilliland, Lafreniere and Harvey (2014, p. 11): 'we are following the lead of Sherry Olson, whose pioneering work on nineteenth-century Montreal is a model of spatial history'; their n. 31 lists her 'foundational studies'. That chapter is not independent: Gilliland was her MAP collaborator. Contested: Sweeny, MAP's co-director (Digital Studies, 2009), argues that 'The ontology of geographic information systems is antithetical to historical understanding', that a GIS ensures 'the illusion of accuracy', and that 'an historical GIS works because it is a-historical'. This is a critique of the instrument from inside the project, not of Olson. Not a founding: the editors give the US and British national repositories as 'some of the most important work in the field' (p. xi), and the strand's Gregory and Southall (1998) is a separate, aggregate-boundary tradition. 'Pioneering' is the Victoria team's word, not this entry's.

edges.relationship: City building in long swings: Baltimore's growth read through cycles of investment, construction and neighbourhood change (1979–80), and Montreal's through its builders and migrants (1997–2011)
edges.evidence_note: In-period, her own words. Baltimore (1980; introduction and acknowledgments read): 'There is a tempo and a pattern to urban growth'; 'City growth is a boom-and-bust sequence of "long swings," with eighteen years or so separating the neighboring peaks. This applies equally to North America and Europe over at least two centuries'; 'This book is about city building, an internal dynamic of the city-state, and how Baltimoreans see themselves and their situation. In that sense, Baltimore is America, in its rhythm of building up and tearing down, swarming and dispersing' (pp. ix–x). She names what the book leaves out: 'The most serious gap is our ignorance of the lives of slaves and servants in Baltimore', the Polish Catholic community, and 'the strategies of landowners and real estate investors in each round' (pp. ix–x). The acknowledgments record that 'David Harvey shared his discovery of Baltimore for several years' (p. vii). The 1979 Annals article (abstract only): 'The long-swing rhythm of urban investment has produced distinctive spaces and forms in the city', with 'a tempo and a spatial matrix for income redistribution, social conflict, and social pathology'. Montreal (1997, read in full): migration 'Récurrentes de 20 ans en 20 ans' (p. 81); half the population lived within a kilometre of the centre in 1861, in the next ring by 1881 and the one beyond by 1901, as the building trades, 'telle une vague déferlante, se déplacent vers la périphérie' (p. 89). Reception. In-period reviews of Baltimore appeared in the AHR, JAH, Technology and Culture and JEH (1981) and in JIH and the Journal of Historical Geography (1982); none could be read here (JSTOR, OUP and Elsevier walls; the JEH first-page preview image was illegible), so no in-period judgement is reported. Later readings, snippet witnesses (opening paragraphs only): Sager (CHR, 2012) reads Peopling the North American City (2011, unread here) as 'an example of the research collaboratory that has emerged in recent decades'; Horner (HS/SH, 2013) says it 'makes a vital contribution not only to the historiography of Montreal and Quebec, but also to the way that historians and geographers conceptualize the relationship between individuals, families, communities and urban space'. A contribution to the field's building-and-space strand beside Warner, not a new school.

edges.relationship: Schooling, school inspection and the census studied as state formation in the Canadas: education as 'government of the self' (1988), inspection as the making of 'relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (1992), the census as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001); work that predates the framework, and that Christie later cites for the point that McKay describes governmentality (2009)
edges.evidence_note: In-period reviews, read in full; Curtis's books are unread, so his words are the reviewers' quotations with their page references. Davey (Historical Studies in Education 1, 1989, pp. 161–165) on Building the Educational State (1988): 'one of the great strengths of Curtis' approach is his grounding of Foucault's analysis of power and subjectivity within a marxist theory of state formation and cultural forms' (p. 161); he quotes Curtis that 'the construction of the Educational State was accomplished only through the destruction of a prior educational organization and the marginalization of the structure of educational possibilities' (book p. 15), that schooling meant 'the anchoring of the conditions of political governance in the selves of the governed' (no page given), that education 'was not a means to government; education was government: government of the self' (book p. 110) and that 'public education was administered into dominance only through a myriad of local struggles' (book p. 132); Davey notes 'there is no reference to Gramsci or the theory of hegemony in the bibliography or the index' (p. 162) and objects that Curtis 'fails to provide an adequate account of patriarchal relations in the period' (p. 165). Miller (Historical Studies in Education 5, 1993, pp. 123–126) on True Government by Choice Men? (1992) quotes 'Educational inspection was about state formation: the creation, stabilization and normalisation of relations of power, authority, domination and exploitation' (book p. 32) and 'Bureaucratic administration was seen by political liberals as practical education, a ‘normal school’ for the people' (book p. 7); she says Curtis 'carefully distances himself' from a social-control argument (p. 124) and regrets 'the relative invisibility of gender relations' (p. 125). Bryan Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, pp. 365–367): 'In their purpose they can only be applauded; but their search is at times disturbingly narrow' (p. 365); as a 'model' Curtis's account 'is overstated to the point of distorting actual historical relations in the evolution of state and civil society' (p. 366); yet he credits Curtis and Colonial Leviathan with 'the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366). Later readings: Belshaw (2002, read) quotes the census book: 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305). Christie (Underhill Review 2009, read): 'Here I think we need to be alert to Bruce Curtis's important point that what McKay is really describing is governmentality'; this is Christie's characterisation, and Curtis's own 2009 chapter ('After ‘Canada’') is unread. The edge records a contribution to the strand the atlas calls 'State formation before the framework'; the work predates McKay's prospectus (2000, unread beyond its abstract), and no checked text by McKay names Curtis. The collaboration with Philip Corrigan (1985) is title-level; the moral regulation entry treats this state-formation work as shared ground (edge_848), so no separate Curtis edge to moral_regulation is drawn.

edges.relationship: Census returns read as artefacts of state knowledge rather than transparent records: objections to inferring property, gender and inheritance from the 1871 Ontario census in a review of Darroch and Soltow (1996), and census making as 'the making of things to be taken' (2001)
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Curtis's 1996 review of Gordon Darroch and Lee Soltow's census study of property in Ontario (1994) and his census history (2001); it is not a verdict on quantitative history as a whole, and Darroch and Soltow are not in the atlas. His own words (Historical Studies in Education 8, 1996, pp. 107–110, read in full): 'Anyone who has worked with manuscript census data must be impressed with the meticulous and painstaking analysis undertaken here' (p. 109); 'Two related critical points seem worth making about census artifacts and the matter of gender' (p. 109); the authors 'go so far as to suggest that their cross-sectional study is actually longitudinal' (p. 109); 'The census simply cannot tell us much about the value of distributed property, about the gendered distribution of property, certainly nothing about inheritance patterns, although, as an ideological practice, census-taking attached property to adult men' (pp. 109–110); and, qualifying, 'the book is an important contribution to ongoing debates' (p. 110). The census book (2001) is unread; as Belshaw quotes it (2002, read), 'Census making ... is not in any simple sense the taking of things as they are; in an important sense it is the making of things to be taken' (book p. 305), and it 'seeks to tie individuals within an administrative grid and then to hold them steady so that they may become objects of knowledge and government' (book p. 26). Belshaw's reading, in his words: 'Historical demographers know that the census is far from perfectly reliable but, after reading Bruce Curtis’ latest book, many more will be mindful of how political it is throughout', and 'demographic and social historians may ignore Curtis’ findings at their peril'. Kind: critique, because the 1996 text objects to inferences drawn from census returns; it is not a rejection of quantitative work, and Curtis calls the book he reviews an important contribution.

edges.relationship: Rural Lower Canada as a feudal, household-centred peasant society, neither routine-bound nor market-rational, into which wage labour in the fur and timber trades was fitted (1981–85); and the rebellion of 1837 as a rural popular movement (1993, known through reviews)
edges.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full): 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); against the commercial reading of Paquet and Wallot, cited in n. 16, 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue', while 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); subdivision of holdings followed 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16). Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) is unread; its publisher describes rural Quebec as 'essentially organized around a feudal society', with 'a pronounced pattern of household self-sufficiency' in three Lower Richelieu parishes (lof_greer_1985). His 1981 Sorel study rejected the 'atavistic mentality' explanation of the rural crisis; that critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989 and is not repeated here. The Patriots and the People (1993) is unread. Reviewers' words, not his: Dessureault (1998, read for evidence-quebec.md) says it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes', finds the struggle fed by 'une forme de républicanisme populaire' (p. 206), places Greer 'dans une perspective marxiste anticolonialiste, héritière de l'œuvre pionnière de Stanley B. Ryerson' (p. 205) and objects that he 'réfute l'existence de clivages socio-économiques à l'intérieur même de la paysannerie' (p. 207); Cardinal (1999) writes that 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien' (p. 185). Ouellet's review essay on the book (Histoire sociale / Social History 28, 1995) is unread (browser check), so his reply is not quoted and no fernand_ouellet edge is drawn. Rudin (1995) names Greer among the révisionnistes.

edges.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
edges.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.

edges.relationship: Settler colonialism historicised as one mode of colonial invasion among several, beside imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism, dominant in some periods and regions of northern North America and not others: a sympathetic critique that keeps Wolfe's 'structure, not an event' (2018–19)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, all after 2000 and dated. 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (Journal of the CHA 30, 2019, read in full; a CHA keynote): settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians', but over 500 years of invasion 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the danger of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory' and, with Wolfe, settler colonialism is 'a structure, not an event'; 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); and 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' (p. 79). Property and Dispossession (2018), introduction read on Cambridge Core (no page markers): 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006). The target is the field, not patrick_wolfe: Greer accepts Wolfe's structure thesis and objects to how the term is commonly used, citing Woolford and Benvenuto's warning that it risks becoming 'a reductive shorthand' (p. 63). The William and Mary Quarterly essay (2019) is unread beyond its recorded opening.

edges.relationship: In a critique of Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, the staples tradition's trade-centred economy faulted for confining attention to relations of exchange and passing over the household subsistence production that, he argued, made up most of early Canada's economy (1985)
edges.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full), in a critique of H. C. Pentland's Labour and Capital in Canada, 1650–1860 (written 1960, published 1981), which is not an atlas entry: Pentland 'follows the lead of his Toronto mentors in conflating the Canadian economy and its overseas trade'; 'While Innis, Creighton, and their contemporary disciples confine their attention to relations of exchange, however, Pentland at least focuses on the ‘social relations of production’', so 'it seems fair to regard him as the labour historian of the staples school' (p. 9). The subsistence producers who were most of the population 'were therefore scarcely of interest to bourgeois theorists from Adam Smith to Harold Innis and Clare Pentland. For these last two, ‘the colonial economy’ meant the meagre flow of commodities' (p. 21). His counter-claim is stated as an untested estimate: 'No one has yet made a serious attempt to measure the value of the colony's annual production of all goods'; 'If they did, I have no doubt that the aggregate agricultural output would embody vastly more labour than all the furs and squared timbers and other ‘staple products’' (p. 20). Qualifications kept: Pentland 'deserves high marks for posing the important questions and for assembling valuable information' (p. 8). The arrow stands for this passage of a review essay aimed chiefly at Pentland; Greer names Innis and Creighton as the staples school but does not review their books. Note 2 (p. 8) also discusses Kealey's and Palmer's use of Pentland; that is not drawn as an edge.

edges.relationship: British Columbia's reserve system explained as geographical dispossession: a capacity resting on state-backed force, a momentum from capital and settlers, a legitimation in a discourse of civilization and savagery, and a management by 'disciplinary technologies' of maps, numbers, law and the land system (1997–2004); written in a settler society's terms ('successful settler colonialism', 2003), with no derivation from Wolfe's theory established by the texts checked, and faulted by reviewers for few Native voices
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Revisiting the Native Land Question', BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 137–151, his précis of Making Native Space, read in full: the reserves comprised 'slightly more than one-third of 1 per cent of provincial land' (p. 137); 'The capacity to dispossess rested on raw firepower authorized, usually, by the administrative superstructure of the state. … The momentum to dispossess came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods' (p. 137); 'The legitimation of dispossession lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery … the implementation of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies among which maps, numbers, and, especially, the common law were essential' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia. One is about progress and development … It rests, however, on the other basic story about this place, which is about dispossession, loss, marginalization, and the struggle for survival' (p. 140); 'Given the values and benefits associated with successful settler colonialism, many British Columbians will find this an exceedingly difficult commitment' (p. 144, of a politics of difference). The 2004 abstract (publisher's abstract via OpenAlex; article unread) states the same four conclusions: 'the initial ability to dispossess rested primarily on physical power and the supporting infrastructure of the state; the momentum to dispossess derived from the interest of capital in profit and of settlers in forging new livelihoods; the legitimation of and moral justification for dispossession lay in a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery …; and the management of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important.' In-period reception. Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia, BC Studies 117 (1998), pp. 64–67, read in full: Harris 'locates the non-Native settlement of British Columbia explicitly in the context of the expansion of European imperial and commercial power' and sees colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space that was formerly theirs into an immigrant society' (p. 64); but 'there are very few "Native voices" in it - something Harris himself admits', and Native peoples, 'despite a few examples to the contrary, emerge as victims' (p. 66); in the later chapters 'the connections to colonization … increasingly fade away' and class is not discussed (pp. 66–67); still 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67). Daniel Clayton, BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 5–11, read in full: 'Harris's most political work to date and arguably the most significant contribution to our understanding of colonialism in the province since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6). Jo-Anne Fiske, commentary in the 2003 forum (pp. 151–155, read): he 'says little … of how a change in mindset and a marshalling of political will might be achieved', and what he says of the symbolic 'is unsettling in its apparent simplicity' (p. 152); the powers he describes 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152). Harris replied: 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161). Val Napoleon (2004): see pe139_harris_rel_07. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: they cite Merivale, Kymlicka and Macklem, not Wolfe, and the books are unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Harris wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later reading, labelled: Perry (BC Studies 190, 2016, p. 112) says her 2001 book read British Columbia 'within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books'. A Bounded Land (2020), with its 'Postscript: The Boundaries of Settler Colonialism', is cited at title level only.

edges.relationship: Colonialism read through its geographies: the land system as a 'spatial discipline' that bounded Native movement, and the reserve line as the 'primal line on the land' of British Columbia (1997–2003), which Clayton (2003) offered as a model of 'colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire'
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 2003 forum précis (p. 138, read): 'From a Native perspective, an even more enveloping discipline may have been imposed by an introduced land system and its associated settlement geography, which, by controlling where they could and could not go, increasingly bounded and channeled their movements.' The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) is unread; Loo (1998, p. 65, read) quotes it: the land system '[imposing] a spatial discipline with a profound capacity to modify Native life' (p. 101), and by 1881 'Native power over the Lower Mainland and, to a considerable extent, earlier Native lifeworlds had collapsed' (p. 102); Loo: 'According to Harris, in British Columbia disciplinary power rested on the land system (Chapters 3 and 4). To me, this is the heart of Harris's argument … the links between colonization and geographical change are most visible' (p. 65). Making Native Space (2002) is unread; Clayton (2003, read) quotes Harris's aim to tell 'the colonial construction of space in British Columbia' (p. 6, citing pp. xxi, xxviii) and his view that the reserve line 'became, in a sense, the primal line on the land of British Columbia, the one that facilitated or constrained all others' (p. 7); Napoleon (2004, p. 116, read) quotes the reserves 'displayed rather like insects on pins' (p. 271) and their 'fixed place in the Cartesian space of the survey system and in the minds of officials and settlers'. Disciplinary reception (Clayton, a geographer who began working with Harris as a UBC graduate student, p. 6): Harris is 'very much the historian's geographer' (p. 5); the book 'will be more widely read and appreciated for what it says about the spatiality of colonialism, or what Harris sees as colonialism's "geographical core" (xxiv)' (p. 7); he offers '(however unwittingly) a powerful and important programme for a postcolonial historical geography that significantly departs from current critical norms' (p. 7), 'a timely and potent model for the critical appreciation of colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire' (p. 11), Clayton's contrast with work that 'fixates on the formal disciplinary links between geography and empire' (p. 7). Qualifications: Clayton thinks Harris 'insulate[s]' his historical geography 'from some potentially fruitful comparative lines of inquiry and a fuller digging into theory' (p. 9); the existing spatialhistory row records that the analysis of Merivale and imperial policy 'is not Indigenous testimony'. Distinct from edge 1, which carries the explanation of dispossession in the settler-colonial field; this edge carries the spatial method as historical geography. Compare edge_693 (post → geography, Said in Driver's 'geography's empire').

edges.relationship: The 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era British Columbia, as anthropologists and Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977) held it, questioned: it 'needs to be approached very cautiously', since epidemics, violence and depopulation accompanied the fur trade's wealth (1997–98)
edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia', BC Studies 115/116 (1997/98), pp. 45–82, read at pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82. The position: Fisher, influenced by Wilson Duff's view that the fur trade 'did not destabilize Native life' and by 'his own sharp reaction to the effacement of Native peoples implicit in the "fatal impact" approach', wrote 'a remarkable and influential book — Contact and Conflict — [arguing] that Europeans and Natives met as equals on the Northwest Coast, that contact violence has been considerably exaggerated, and that an infusion of wealth created a brief high point in Northwest Coast culture' (pp. 46–47); 'Fisher's conclusions summarized and extended the prevailing anthropological understanding of the previous generation — a set of assumptions often loosely labelled the cultural enrichment hypothesis, after a phrase first used by Joyce Wike' (p. 47); 'now, twenty years later, new information is available, Native voices have repoliticized issues of land and colonial appropriation, and the intellectual climate has changed' (p. 47). The critique: 'the cultural enrichment hypothesis needs to be approached very cautiously. Crudely applied, it quickly becomes Eurocentric and far too simple. It tends to measure cultural achievement against quantitative and materialistic Western values of accumulation' (p. 80); 'There was no one culture and no fixed datum plane against which to measure cultural enrichment'; 'the enrichment hypothesis ignores too much of what was going on along the Northwest Coast during the contact years. Against enrichment measured by poles, feast goods, and the enhanced authority of some chiefs were epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (p. 81). Fur-trade power: traders' 'politics of fear — "respect" or "terror" were the traders' common words' (p. 58). Qualifications kept: 'There is good evidence for all of these developments' (p. 80); 'Native people were anything but passive victims of these new circumstances, some of which they had largely made themselves. They drew hard trading bargains' (p. 81); and he calls Fisher's book 'remarkable and influential'. The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997, unread) makes the same case in its first chapters; Loo (1998, p. 65, read) summarises the Hudson's Bay Company as a 'proto-colonial presence' (p. 34) whose rule, 'though founded on fear and violence, relied on symbolic gesture and theatre'. Clayton (2003, p. 6, read) measures Making Native Space against Contact and Conflict. No reply by Fisher was checked. Scope: a critique of one interpretation of early contact, not of the native–newcomer field or of agency-centred work as such; edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques of the field's framing.

edges.relationship: Colonial-discourse studies criticised for an emphasis on culture that 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'; he proposed explaining 'colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized' instead, while allowing that 'several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights' (2004)
edges.evidence_note: His own words. Abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94:1 (2004), pp. 165–182 (publisher's abstract, read via OpenAlex; article body closed and unread): 'The emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism tends to obscure other forms of colonial power while making it impossible to contextualize the cultural argument and assess its salience. Rather than focusing on texts, systems of signification, and procedures of knowledge generation, as the colonial discourse literature is wont to do, a fuller understanding of colonial powers is achieved by explaining colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized. In so doing, the issue of power is not prejudged'; it ends 'Although no one body of theory explains colonial power, several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights.' The 2003 précis (BC Studies, pp. 137–138, read) gives culture one of four roles, the legitimation of dispossession. Qualifications: he uses the literature he criticises. In 1997–98 (p. 59 n. 39, read) he cites Said's Orientalism as 'The original and most influential discussion' of the European categories of civilized and savage; Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) finds Making Native Space 'Informed by Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Michel Foucault, and E.P. Thompson'. Clayton's reading, labelled as his (2003, read): Harris is 'neither a close student of the imperial imagination nor a slavish follower of the powerful postcolonial theories' (p. 8, Clayton's paraphrase); his findings fuel 'his suspicion of an international postcolonial literature that, in his view, tends to overplay the hands of culture and discourse relative to other forms of power' (pp. 8–9, citing the 2004 essay as forthcoming); yet he 'favours (again however unwittingly) a certain postcolonial narrative' (p. 9) and 'has absorbed a body of ideas about the ascriptive power of colonial discourse … that were initially advanced by Said' (p. 10). No reply from a postcolonial critic was checked.
edges.map_label: Harris: culture overweighted in colonial-discourse studies, 2003–04

edges.relationship: Foucault's sovereign and disciplinary power as Harris's terms for the fur traders' 'politics of fear' and for the colonial land system and its 'disciplinary technologies' (1997–2004), used selectively
edges.evidence_note: His own words. 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, p. 58, read): the traders' retaliations 'in public theatres of power' were 'what Michel Foucault called sovereign power, a sporadic, local, and highly visible seizure of property or life', quoting Discipline and Punish (n. 37); he adds that 'In the Cordillera, such power did not validate a discourse of legal rights and property relations, as it did in Europe.' 2003 précis (p. 138, read) and 2004 abstract: the management of dispossession by 'disciplinary technologies'. In-period readers. Loo (1998, read): the HBC's power was 'what Harris, following Michel Foucault, calls "sovereign power"', and 'the resettlement of British Columbia turned on "disciplinary power,"' which in British Columbia 'rested on the land system' (p. 65); the book 'is shaped by his reading of a diverse and complex international theoretical literature on power' (p. 64). Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) names Foucault with Fanon, Said and Thompson. Qualification: Clayton (2003, p. 9, read) reports that Harris never '"lets theory loose" in British Columbia, as he puts it (xvii)'. The 1991 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG), which Clayton lists among his methodological essays (p. 6 n. 3), is unread.

edges.relationship: Val Napoleon's review of Making Native Space (2004): the book 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history', its proposals needed 'contemporary Aboriginal voices', and grounding Aboriginal rights in 'difference' is problematic, since Aboriginal peoples 'still have a special place in Canada' whether or not they are 'the same as everyone else'
edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Val Napoleon's review (BC Studies 141, Spring 2004, pp. 114–118, read in full), not a verdict of the Indigenous history field, whose roster also lists Harris as a historian. Her criticisms: 'Harris recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history as it unfolded for roughly a century' (p. 115); Part 4, 'Land and Livelihood', is 'somewhat incongruous with the rest of the book' because there he moves from the archival record to argument (p. 117); the politics of difference is 'nonetheless problematic' (p. 117), and 'Speaking as a First Nations person, I do not believe that it matters whether Aboriginal people are the same as everyone else; we still have a special place in Canada' (p. 117); 'In my view, where historical enquiry gives way to thought about the future, Harris should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices into his discussion … It is from within the experience of this conflicted and contradictory milieu that strategies for future change must be developed and tested, not from without' (p. 117); he does not address 'the structural economic problems that small communities are encountering' (p. 115). Her praise, kept: the book gave her 'a much more textured, dynamic, and human sense of BC history' (p. 116); 'What I appreciate most … is Harris's argument that the colonial approach to land was less about legal or moral principles than about the varying self-interests of the colonizers' (p. 117); it is 'a valuable resource for both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal peoples', and she has 'recommended the book to people from several different Aboriginal communities' (p. 118). She also summarises, without quotation, the Canadian Geographer review symposium of five geographers (47:1, 2003, unread here): they suggested that Harris had '(1) appropriated the voices of patriarchy and of the colonizer' and '(5) insufficiently considered Aboriginal resistance to the reserve allocation system' (pp. 114–115), and Harris replied that 'A book … can only do so much' and 'remains unconvinced that the basic settler attitudes were gendered' (p. 115, her words). Loo (1998, p. 66, read) had made the related point that 'there are very few "Native voices"' in the 1997 book (edge 1). A field-to-person critique naming its proxy, the pattern used for quebec_historiography → fernand_ouellet.

edges.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.
edges.map_label: Gender, race and a settler colony, 1995–2001

edges.relationship: Race in the history of white women and gender in the Canadian West: the 'scarcity model' and 'volcano theory' of gender imbalance traced to colonial promoters (1995), and white masculinity, mixed-race relationships and assisted female migration in colonial British Columbia read as the making of whiteness (2001)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. '“Oh I’m Just Sick of the Faces of Men”', BC Studies 105/106 (1995), pp. 27–44, read at pp. 27–33 and 42–43: Canadian historians used 'the "scarcity model" (the notion that women's experience improves commensurately with their scarcity) and the "volcano theory" of male sexuality (the assumption of a fixed quantity of male sexual energy)' (p. 27); 'a quarter-century of inquiry into women's history has produced little on the effect of a skewed demography on women's experience' (p. 28); its 'most clear example' is Jan Noel's 'New France: Les femmes favorisées' (p. 29 n. 4); both models 'are based on essentialist understandings of both sexuality and race. Practitioners of the "scarcity model" never compute aboriginal women (or, for that matter, men) into their arithmetical evaluation' (p. 30); they are 'integral not only to twentieth century scholarship, but also to colonial discourse itself' (p. 31), descending from Wakefield and the colonial promoters (p. 32); white women's experience 'was never determined by gender alone. British Columbia was a class society' (p. 42); 'While gender imbalance increased white women's opportunities for heterosexual contact, it restricted those economic and social possibilities not contained within the heterosexual nexus' (p. 43). On the Edge of Empire (2001) is unread; Orlowski (p. 119) quotes its aim, 'the importance of race to the social experience of gender in nineteenth-century British Columbia' (p. 8), and 'a sharp disjuncture between colonial discourse and colonial practice on this edge of empire' (p. 167, quoted p. 120; Carter, p. 119, uses the same phrase). In-period reception, read in full: Carter (2002): 'This book also makes a valuable Canadian contribution to "Whiteness" studies' (p. 117); Rutherdale (2002): 'At the heart of this imagined community was Whiteness' (p. 325), and the reformers' hope that white women were the 'imperial panacea' (p. 4, as quoted p. 326). Critics: Orlowski (2002) holds that she 'fails to invoke what Roediger calls the "wages of whiteness"', leaving 'a binary racial divide that runs through the entire book but did not run through colonial British Columbia', with Chinese labourers set aside (p. 121), and that her claim that 'class relations are central to social relations' receives little attention (p. 121); Carter (p. 119) asks for the North American setting ('This edge of empire had much in common with California'); Rutherdale's 'small quibble' is that the 'Home' and 'Away' relationship 'could be further probed' (p. 326). Distinct from the Van Kirk packet's edges on fur-trade women: this edge is the post-fur-trade settler colony and the critique of the scarcity model.

edges.relationship: Mixed-race relationships not to be explained by white women's absence: Perry's 1995 criticism of fur-trade historians, Van Kirk's 'brilliant account' included, for treating intermarriage as the product of that absence, and her 2001 argument (as Carter reports it) that such relationships were 'not confined to the fur trade' and that 'happy stories' of fur-trade marriages can 'obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism'
edges.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 1995 (BC Studies 105/106, read at p. 30): 'Historians of the fur trade, while concerned with establishing the salience of mixed-race relationships, nonetheless explain their frequency as the product of white women's absence'; n. 8: 'For a brilliant account which ultimately suggests that the existence of mixed-race relationships was the result of white women's absence from the fur trade, see Sylvia Van Kirk, "Many Tender Ties" … Also see Jennifer S. H. Brown, Strangers in Blood … and Robin Fisher, Contact and Conflict'; n. 11 quotes Van Kirk: 'Had it been possible for fur traders to bring their wives out at an earlier date, it is doubtful whether intermarriage with native women would have been so extensive' (Many Tender Ties, p. 173); the 'volcano theory' 'holds that mixed-race relationships are at worst unfathomable and at best the products of abnormal historical circumstances' (p. 30). Qualifications kept: the criticism is of one explanation, not of the field; she calls Van Kirk's account 'brilliant' (p. 30 n. 8) and 'pioneering' (p. 43), and relies on it for the displacement of Aboriginal women (p. 43). 2001: the book is unread; Carter (BC Studies 136, p. 118, read) reports that 'Perry does not write a history of these relationships, noting the difficulties with available sources, but she does argue that they were not confined to the fur trade and could be found in the city, in the country, and in mining towns', and that she 'stresses the need to look beyond the "happy stories," such as the long marriage of James Douglas and Amelia Connolly, that can "obscure both coercive details and the larger brutality of colonialism" (62)'. In-period counterpoint: Orlowski (2002, p. 121, read) faults the book because 'the mixed-race couples in colonial B.C. had much to do with building alliances, sometimes between Hudson's Bay Company officers and the daughters of Aboriginal chiefs, a strategy that is not considered at all in the book'. No reply by Van Kirk or Brown was checked. Later reading, labelled: in 2016 (p. 113) she proposes thinking 'seriously about fur-trade colonialism as a distinct and meaningful practice of empire' (Colonial Relations, on the Douglas–Connolly family, is unread). Target: Van Kirk's person entry, since the criticism is of her explanation of intermarriage; her entry cites Perry's 2008 essay on her work only as a later reading.
edges.map_label: Perry: mixed-race unions beyond white women's absence, 1995–2001

edges.relationship: Feminist and postcolonial work on gender, race and colonial categories (Stoler and McClintock, as she and her reviewers name them, with Said and Burton) as the 'international literature on gender and colonialism' that she said inspired On the Edge of Empire (2001), used with a caution about analysing 'white discourse and white discourse alone' (1995)
edges.evidence_note: Her own words. 2001 (BC Studies 132, p. 58, read): the book 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism'; 'Edward Said's Orientalism contains the germinal insight that such stock knowledge functioned to inform and serve the centre rather than to understand the various peripheries about which, putatively, it spoke' (pp. 58–59); Burton's argument, as Perry puts it, that knowledge of margins should 'unpack the intimate wedding of historical scholarship to the nation-state' (p. 59, citing Burton in Catherine Hall's Cultures of Empire reader); Anne McClintock's 'anachronistic space' (p. 61); Chakrabarty 'convincingly argues' that history cannot be disaggregated 'from the politics of Western supremacy that produced it' (pp. 63–64). 1995 (p. 43, read), on scholars of colonial discourse who 'analyse white discourse and white discourse alone': the position 'contains an important critique of the intellectual conceit' in historians' attempts to represent the colonized, but 'it can also function to legitimize the neglect of First Nations histories'. In-period reviewers, their characterisations: Rutherdale (Labour/Le Travail 50, 2002, p. 325, read): 'Influenced by the work of Anne Laura Stoler, Perry argues that because "white and Aboriginal people shared ties, homes, children, and labour," they "challenged colonialism's foundational fiction"' (p. 123 of the book), and the book is 'informed by an international post-colonial, feminist, gendered, and Marxist analysis'; Orlowski (Left History 8:1, 2002, pp. 119–120, read): she is 'positioned within feminist postcolonial scholars such as Ann Laura Stoler, Robert J. C. Young, and Anne McClintock, all of whom she refers to in the book', and she uses 'discourse' in 'the Foucauldian sense', though she 'never defines' it (p. 121). The book itself is unread, so the influence of Stoler rests on the reviewers' statements. Stoler, McClintock and Burton have no atlas entries; Stoler is on the post roster (colonial_intimacies) and the gender roster (colonial_categories), Said has a person entry.
